tagline.text: Twin waterfalls on the slopes of Valencia where water spills over red and orange rock

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300~900 (including round-trip transport from Dumaguete, per person)

children.text: Set in Barangay Malabo in Valencia, on the slopes of Mount Talinis, this waterfall tumbles down a rock wall stained red and orange. About 30 minutes from Dumaguete, it makes an easy half-day trip combined with Casaroro Falls and the Red Rock hot spring.

Pulangbato Falls is in Barangay Malabo, Valencia, Negros Oriental. Pulangbato means "red rock" in the local language, and the falls are also called Malabo Falls. The water comes down from the upper Okoy River on the slopes of Mount Talinis (the Cuernos de Negros), and the falls are roughly 30 minutes by road from downtown Dumaguete.
The color of the rock is what sets this place apart. A small first cascade runs over a gray wall, and above it the main drop flows over rock stained red and orange. Guides give the height as around
9m

(about 30 feet), and below it lies a deep, gently sloping green pool. A second, clear and narrow stream falls in the same gorge, which is why the site is sometimes called twin falls. Most explanations attribute the red color to sulfur and minerals carried by geothermal water from Mount Talinis, while some say iron. No geological study has been published, so take this as a rough explanation only.

The usual way to reach the entrance is to take a shared jeepney or multicab from Dumaguete to Valencia, then a motorbike taxi (habal-habal) or tricycle for the last stretch uphill. Sulfur steam rises from the mountainside along the road with a distinctive smell, a reminder that Mount Talinis is a potentially active volcano.
The entrance fee used to be about ₱20, but recent guides list

for adults. There are lockers, tables and cottages, so it is a good spot for families to spread a mat and relax. There are no lifeguards and the submerged rocks are sharp, so it is best not to dive. Combine it with Casaroro Falls and the Red Rock sulfur hot spring in Valencia and the Twin Lakes in Sibulan for a full mountain day trip from Dumaguete. First-time visitors should leave early: the pool is small and can be crowded with local families on weekend afternoons, while on a weekday morning you can look at the red rock wall and take photos in peace. It is not a large tourist site, but the unusual rock color and the short distance from Dumaguete make it a good place to enjoy nature in a short time.

blocks.title: Main falls stained red and orange

children.text: The water starts above a gray rock wall and runs down rock stained red and orange. The color is rare for a waterfall and makes for good photos. The color looks sharpest in the late morning when the sun hits it.

Next to the red falls, a clear, narrow stream drops separately. The contrast between the two colors is fun to look at. The area is said to have kept a natural atmosphere because it has not been heavily developed.

Swimming is allowed in the pool below the falls. The water is clear and cold. However, there is no lifeguard, the submerged rocks are sharp and the pool is shallow in places, so stay careful near the shallow edges.

blocks.title: Sulfur steam along the mountain road

children.text: Sulfur steam rises from the slope along the road to the falls. The smell is strong, but it gives you the feeling of passing through the middle of volcanic country. Many visitors stop for a photo.
A few minutes down the road from the falls is the Red Rock hot spring. You can soak in warm sulfur water of about
, and the separate entrance fee is around
. It is a good place to unwind after swimming at the falls.
There are lockers, tables and cottages near the entrance, so you can leave your things and relax. Many local visitors bring food to eat with family and friends.
It is close to Dumaguete and lies in the same direction as Casaroro Falls and the Twin Lakes, so they are easy to combine. With a rental car or motorbike you can visit two or three sites in one day.

items.title: Half-day route from Dumaguete
items.subtitle: Falls and hot spring in one go

children.text: Board a jeepney or multicab to Valencia near the Dumaguete public market. The ride takes about
20~30 minutes
In Valencia, switch to a motorbike taxi or tricycle and head up to the falls entrance in Malabo. Stop for a photo at the sulfur steam section along the way.
Pay the entrance fee and walk down to the falls. Take photos first in the quiet morning, then enjoy swimming in the shallow areas.
Change out of wet clothes and move on to the Red Rock sulfur hot spring for a warm soak.
Have lunch in Valencia town and return to Dumaguete. Return jeepneys thin out in the afternoon, so leave early.

If you also want to see Casaroro Falls, a motorbike or rental car is more convenient, and it is better to plan a full day. After rain, the road can be slippery and the water muddy, so postponing the trip a day is an option.

items.title: Full-day mountain route
items.subtitle: Three waterfalls and a lake in one day

children.text: Leave Dumaguete by rental car or motorbike toward Valencia.
Go down the steps of Casaroro Falls to see the jungle waterfall first.
Move on to Pulangbato Falls to see the red rock and the pool.
Rest and have lunch at the Red Rock hot spring.
Head up toward Sibulan to see the Twin Lakes viewpoint, then come back down to Dumaguete before sunset.

From the airport, take a tricycle or taxi to central Dumaguete, then board a jeepney toward Valencia.
From Cebu, you can also use the short ferry crossing between Liloan port and Sibulan. Check timetables locally.

Return jeepneys become scarce in the late afternoon, and one source puts the last one at around 5 PM. It is safer to head back early.
It takes about 20 to 30 minutes by car from central Dumaguete. The road is narrow and uphill, so only experienced riders should take a motorbike or scooter.
There is parking at the entrance, and older sources list a parking fee of

In your navigation app, search for Pulangbato Falls or Malabo Falls. The signal can be weak on mountain roads, so download an offline map.
The dry season from December to May is the best time. The water is clear and the path is less slippery.
In the rainy season, rain can swell the water and turn it muddy, which changes how the red color looks. After heavy rain, check local conditions before you set out.

Within the day, early morning until before noon is best. There are fewer people, the sun lights up the red rock so the color looks vivid, and public transport back is easier. On weekends, holidays and in peak season, visitors crowd in during the afternoon and the pool can get busy.

The easiest option is to stay in central Dumaguete and make a round trip. Dumaguete has lodging at every price level and a seaside promenade that is pleasant in the evening. There are few large places to stay around the falls, so a day trip is recommended.

For meals, small stalls and cottages near the entrance can handle simple food, and there are restaurants in Valencia town. It is convenient to bring food and water in advance. Please take your trash back with you.

For dinner back in Dumaguete, restaurants along the promenade and local eateries in town are convenient. Many people also book a massage near their lodging to ease tired muscles after a full day of swimming and travel. In peak season you may need reservations, so check ahead whether your lodging and restaurants are open.
The water may stain clothing, so wear dark colors.
Bring swimwear, a towel and a change of clothes, and use a locker for convenience.
Non-slip sandals or water shoes are best. The rocks are sharp and slippery.
Return jeepneys thin out in the afternoon, so be back by about 3 PM at the latest.
Agree on the motorbike taxi price first, and also discuss whether the driver will wait for the return trip.
Combine it with Casaroro Falls, the Red Rock hot spring and the Twin Lakes for an efficient full-day plan.
Bring plenty of cash in small bills. The entrance and the hot spring may not accept cards.
A small waterproof bag or zip-top bag helps protect your phone and wallet.
Follow local signs and staff instructions, and since opening hours are said to differ by day of the week, confirm them on site.
When taking photos below the falls, do not stand on wet rock, and keep your phone in a waterproof case. If you are with children, it is safer to bring life jackets separately.
There is no lifeguard, the submerged rocks are sharp and the water is shallow in places, so do not dive into the pool.
During or right after heavy rain the water can swell and become dangerous, so avoid entering the water.
Mount Talinis is a potentially active volcanic area and sulfur steam comes from the roadside. The smell is strong, so those with weak lungs should take care.
The steps and rocks on the way to the falls are slippery when wet. Hold children's hands.
Entrance fees and opening hours can change, so check the latest announcements.
Leave valuables in a locker and do not bring them to the water's edge.
People with sensitive skin should rinse off with clean water after swimming because of the sulfur. Be careful not to get the water in your eyes.
